title: SOC 2 Without Security Is Just Security Theater
summary: A SOC 2 report without real security is just security theater. Learn the red flags in SOC 2 audits and the questions to ask before you sign with an auditor.
body_markdown:
The CEO of one of the most reputable auditors in the compliance space recently participated in an interview where she put into words the exact reason I cofounded Oneleet.


In an[episode of the Responsible Disclosure podcast](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=59ISaaZNgeU) , Avani Desai, CEO of[Schellman](https://www.schellman.com/) , states, “The perception of trust is actually a lot more dangerous than no trust at all.” At Oneleet, we call that security theater. It generates a perception of trust without any substance, which is worse than having no trust.


In the compliance world, this looks like a SOC 2 report symbolizing tight security controls that work. And that isn’t always the case.


## Security Theater from an Auditor’s Perspective


Security theater is performative security. It’s prioritizing ticking boxes on a compliance checklist rather than focusing on what really matters: security. When you focus on compliance, you miss the point. When you focus on security, compliance follows.


Desai notes a few examples of security theater. A “no-touch audit” where the auditor doesn’t request evidence. Paying $1,000 for a speedy SOC 2 report. These are red flags for auditors. They agree that the industry has lost sight of the purpose behind SOC 2: real security.


Hearing a trusted, reputable auditor state this is validating for me as a founder of a company fighting security theater. It also gives me hope that we can refocus the industry on what actually matters: security.


## Where the Compliance Industry Falls Short


Desai names the root problem directly: There’s a disconnect between compliance and security. At some point, the goal of compliance became getting a piece of paper as fast as possible so your sales team can close the deal. And security (the thing that piece of paper is supposed to represent) became optional.


Compliance software has made that disconnect more prominent. The industry has done a great job of automating the parts of SOC 2 that should be automated (think evidence collection). But most of that software is built to get you to the report. It can’t tell you whether that control actually makes your business more secure.


It’s why we built Oneleet the way we did.


We involve humans in the process to augment the work our platform does. A former auditor tests controls and ensures they’re relevant to your business. A pentester tries to break in. A[real vCISO](https://www.oneleet.com/blog/meet-your-oneleet-vciso) helps fix findings. *Then* an independent auditor comes in to verify. By the time the independent auditor comes into the process, the security work has already been done, so the report reflects security you actually have. It gives meaning to the badge.


## Questions to Ask Before Signing with an Auditor


In her interview, Desai references a few red flags in the industry to look out for, and they are questions founders should ask before signing with an auditor.


Who signs the report, and can you verify their reputation?


Does the firm ever report exceptions (when an auditor reports they tested a control and found it didn’t work as described), or does every report come back clean? (That question is critical. Exceptions mean they’re looking. Clean reports every time reek of rubber-stamp checkmarks.)


## “Compliance Is a Byproduct of Security”


This is a direct quote from one of Desai’s interviewers, and it’s a quote that we have said from day one when starting Oneleet. If you prioritize security, passing SOC 2 follows. If your goal is to pass the audit, you won’t be secure. Compliance is a natural byproduct of security.


Forward-thinking companies that prioritize security will open new deals and markets faster than those who get SOC 2 just to have a badge. It has already become a differentiator for enterprise buyers who trust you with their security (and their reputation).


The work required to get compliant and get secure overlaps more than most people think. Why not focus on getting secure, when compliance will naturally follow?


## Making SOC 2 Affordable Without Shortcuts


The cost of getting SOC 2 used to be a blocker for small businesses. Desai quotes $150k as the starting figure for SOC 2 just a few years ago, making it unachievable for small businesses.


That gap is where security theater found its market.


The industry created an environment where cutting corners made SOC 2 possible for small businesses. The idea was that if you focus less on security and more on checking compliance boxes, you can cut costs.


That’s the opposite of how we approach compliance at Oneleet. We set out to make effective security painless, and that doesn’t mean paying more for it. It means spending your time and budget on the parts of SOC 2 that actually protect you. We cut the busywork that slows teams down and drives up costs, not the security controls that keep you safe. You get experts when you need them and one all-in price, with no surprise fees later.


## Continuous Monitoring Is the Future


Desai sparks hope when she states that, for the first time in her career, she sees continuous monitoring as a possibility in the compliance industry. Threat actors don’t stop just because you have a SOC 2 report. Their efforts are continuous, and ours should be, too.


But continuous monitoring is only as good as *what* you’re monitoring. That’s where human judgment comes in. Watch the wrong controls, and you’re arguably worse off than if you weren’t monitoring at all, because now you have a green dashboard that suggests everything is fine. That’s the perception of trust all over again. Watch the right controls, and you stay secure between audits.


That’s what it looks like when security and compliance are connected. The security work comes first, and the compliance report simply reflects it.


Before your next audit, ask yourself whether you’re building security or just preparing for a report. Then, find out exactly who’s signing that report and what they actually test.
